item.text: {"text":"Evidence supports testing the objective before adding semantic capacity. [gSASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.07192) attributes SASRec weaknesses to overconfidence induced by negative sampling; its improvements combine more negatives with generalized BCE, so they do not isolate calibration alone. Reported gains include +9.47% NDCG versus BERT4Rec and 73% less training time on MovieLens-1M—not evidence for this Amazon validation HR@10 task. The [authors’ implementation](https://github.com/asash/gsasrec) recommends 256 negatives and calibration t=0.75; beta=1−t+t·k/(catalogue_size−1). Implement gBCE through the documented positive-logit transformation; simply multiplying positive BCE by beta is not equivalent. Stronger calibration can delay useful learning, making short early-stopping patience misleading.\n\n[Turning Dross Into Gold Loss](https://github.com/antklen/sasrec-bert4rec-recsys23) provides a complementary approach: train SASRec with cross-entropy over the positive and multiple sampled negatives, reusing a user’s negative pool across sequence positions for efficiency. A [2024 analysis, revised in 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07770), shows single-negative categorical cross-entropy and BPR are equivalent, reinforcing the importance of negative count. Practical comparison: unchanged encoder with BCE, gBCE, and sampled cross-entropy at matched negative counts, sampling exclusions, optimizer, and training budget; then compare improvement per GPU-second. Select using the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10 with identical candidate sets and seeds. Training-pair margins cannot establish generalization or diagnose calibration. The retrieved evidence does not establish a winner under this exact Amazon protocol; Electronics’ weak separation motivates the ablation, not a conclusion."}
